name: The Royal Fork
summary: The royal fork, also called the family fork, is a knight fork that checks the enemy king while attacking the queen, winning her outright.
intro: The royal fork is the crown jewel of knight tactics: a single knight leap that attacks the enemy king and queen at the same time. Because the knight gives check, the opponent has no choice but to deal with the king first, and the queen is left to her fate. Also known as the family fork, it wins the strongest piece on the board for nothing at all. Every chess player dreams of landing one, and every chess player must learn to see one coming.
boardCaption: White to move: the knight on d5 leaps to e7 with 1.Ne7+, checking the king on g8 while simultaneously attacking the queen on c8.

sections.heading: The Most Valuable Fork
paragraphs: A fork is any single move that attacks two or more enemy pieces at once, and the knight is the fork's natural specialist. Among all possible forks, one stands above the rest: the fork of king and queen together. Chess players call it the royal fork, or affectionately the family fork, because it rounds up the most important members of the enemy household in one blow.

What makes the royal fork unstoppable is the check. When a knight attacks both king and queen, the rules of chess dictate the response: the check must be answered immediately. The king is forced to move, and the queen simply cannot be saved. On the very next move the knight takes her, converting one clever leap into a decisive material advantage that usually ends the game.

sections.heading: The Example
paragraphs: In the diagram, White's knight sits on d5, with the Black king on g8 and the Black queen on c8. The winning move is 1.Ne7+. From e7, the knight attacks both g8 and c8 at the same time, so this single jump delivers check to the king and attacks the queen simultaneously. It is the royal fork in its purest form.

Black has no good answer. The king cannot capture the knight, nothing else can take it either, so Black must simply move the king with a reply like 1...Kf7. Then comes the harvest: 2.Nxc8, and the knight scoops up the queen. White has won the most powerful piece on the board at no cost, and the rest is a matter of technique.

sections.heading: Spotting Royal Forks
paragraphs: The pattern is pure knight geometry. A knight forks two squares that are each a knight's move away from where it lands. So whenever the enemy king and queen sit a knight's move apart from one common empty square, they are vulnerable: a knight leaping to that square attacks both at once, and because one of them is the king, the leap comes with check.

Train yourself to scan for these squares in every position. When you see the enemy king and queen close together, ask whether any square attacks both and whether your knight can reach it. The same vigilance applies in defense: keep your own king and queen off such geometries, because a royal fork against you is just as unstoppable as one in your favor.

keyIdeas: The royal fork, also called the family fork, is a knight fork attacking the enemy king and queen simultaneously.
Because the fork comes with check, the king must move and the queen cannot be saved.
In the diagram, 1.Ne7+ checks the king on g8 and attacks the queen on c8 at once.
After a forced king move such as 1...Kf7, White wins the queen with 2.Nxc8.
A knight forks any two squares that are each a knight's move from its landing square, so look for one square that hits both king and queen.
Defensively, avoid placing your own king and queen a knight's move away from a common square the enemy knight can reach.
